newsitem.title: UK: Most back N.Ireland talks but doubt success-poll.
newsitem.headline: Most back N.Ireland talks but doubt success-poll.

text.p: Almost all of Northern Ireland's war-weary people want the next British government to push ahead with slow-moving peace talks, but almost as many think the negotiations will fail, an opinion poll showed on Monday.

The survey by Belfast's Queen's University also told the government that wins the May 1 poll that most people want the issue of disarming guerrillas -- the biggest single obstacle to getting talks onto an all-party basis -- relegated to a sub-committee of the negotiations.
The poll, published and commissioned by the Belfast Telegraph, showed that 94 percent of the province's 1.5 million people supported the Belfast peace talks convened by Britain and Ireland last year.

The negotiations, chaired by former U.S. Senator George Mitchell, are supposed to forge a settlement between pro-British Protestant leaders and pro-Irish Catholic nationalists who want Northern Ireland reunited with the Irish republic.

But 74 percent of the population, which is 60 percent Protestant and 40 percent Catholic, doubted that the talks, which resume on June 3, would lead to a negotiated settlement of a 28-year conflict which has killed 3,200.

The survey showed that British Prime Minister John Major's Conservative government and its likely successor, the Labour party of Tony Blair, were out of step with grass roots thinking about the vexed issue of "decommissioning" guerrilla weapons.
It said that 69 percent of those polled want the issue handled by a sub-committee while talks on an overall settlement carry on. The issue is unresolved at the negotiations.

Major's government has softened its stand on disarmament from insisting that Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas disarm to earn a seat at the talks to saying that they must show a willingness to disarm as the negotiations continue.
But the IRA, and its direct opposites, pro-British Loyalist extremists, say that handing over weapons cannot be contemplated until there is an overall political settlement.
The Labour party has pursued a bipartisan approach to Northern Ireland while in opposition and has pledged that there will be no major change if it takes over government.
Sinn Fein, political wing of the IRA, is barred from the negotiations because of the IRA's resumption of its war against British rule last February after a 17-month truce.

Major, speaking after the IRA was blamed for preventing Saturday's running of Britain's favourite horse race, the Grand National steeplechase, said there was little likelihood of Sinn Fein claiming a talks' seat in June because of the incident.
The Conservatives say they want proof that any new IRA truce is a permanent end to violence, not a tactical ploy, and want a "decontamination period" to assess how genuine the truce is.
The poll was taken before the Grand National was disrupted by a bomb scare.

Sinn Fein leaders say they doubt the IRA will call a new truce unless Britain drops all preconditions such as disarmament, sets a time frame for the talks and takes confidence building steps such as freeing IRA prisoners.

The poll showed that most members of the Protestant community, which is thought to be pro-British, do not want Sinn Fein at the talks without a truce while most Catholics want the party at the negotiations immediately.
